chapter: Learning trombone and the Wisconsin Roof years
title: Dave Peyton's band at the Regal, the McKinney battle and the 165th Army band
summary: He describes the Regal band, a battle with McKinney's Cotton Pickers, and his Army band and theater training.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: What was the name of that band then?
Yeah, that was the Boynton Young's band. Oh, yeah.
That's the name of the band?

Yeah. And about this time he had Raymond Valentine on trumpet. And he had Eddie Belfield. You might have heard of him, Eddie Belfield. And Willow Morin, we had a, and a fellow by. Doc? Hmm? Doc Morin?

Doc Willow? Yeah. Yeah. And Raymond Valentine. And we had Cass Simpson on piano and accordion. And we had Boris Lovingood. He's from, I think Austin, Texas. And we had the, we had the, five brass. And I think we had four reeds. Two pianists and Snagg Jones on the drum. So we had a battle with this, the same McKinney's Cotspickers. Don Redman had them then, you heard of Don Redman had them. So they were working out of this Greystone ballroom in Detroit. So they were booked there. We played the Matinee on Sunday and played that evening too. So we knew this coming, we'd been to Detroit and heard the band. We knew they had a good band. So we had three arrangers in the band so we had a whole lot of singing you know. And we played a whole lot of this, all of the college tunes you see. We played like Indiana, you know, really jazz, you see. So that's how we came down to Chicago to play for fraternity you know. And they heard that we played these college tunes. That's how I came to get the job at Savoy. But so we decided, we said well, we'll just play some stocks and just appear mediocre you know. So we came in around, I think it was something around five o'clock, something like that. And they stood around and heard it. So I imagine they said well, hear nothing to this you know. But later on at night when they started playing by the eight o'clock, we showered down to them. So they, down, down taking the band in the back of the dressing room and rehearsed them. Yeah, it was on Easter Sunday, I never forget that. Yeah, he taking that band in the back and we were together, see we've been together about six years. Maybe a man or so you know, in exchange you know. So then it goes after leaves, after leaves, and we went up to Lansing. So I quit him, I was making $110 in 1929, no tax coming out of the regal, you know. And you see my best experience I'd say would be, was the brass band. This 165th band was a wartime band, you know in the Army. And the fellow by the name of Art Stewart, that was a conductor, he was a fellow that had a high soprano voice like, alright, get in there, you know. He frightened the heck out of me to begin with. But then I found out that it wasn't, he didn't mean it, he didn't mean it. So I'd go and rehearse with him every Sunday. And overtures such as morning, noon and night, 1812 and things like. And hot strasses, marches, a whole lot of them tough marches, you know. And so that's when I, my first time in New York was 1924. I went there with the, it was a Nathapithias Convention. And we marched all the way from Harlem to Central Park. And then we camped out on the Boston Road. And that night someone put a huge cross, I didn't burn the cross. But it started raining, see. And they put the cross out. But that morning we was in this pup tent, you know. And that morning it was flooded, it was a ravine, it was down like, you know, down the ravine. And then we marched all the way to a little town I've forgotten how to play in Constance. We were there a week. But that helped me in the theater. Yeah, that helped me in the theater, see. Because when I went to Riva Theater, he heard about me and he featured me playing jazz, but still I had to play my part because we was playing the music for the pitches, no vitaphone then, you know. Yeah, and it was a storm scene, you know, the bass and trombones, whatever was happening, the music was cued that way and you had to play it, see. And then fanfare and everything, such things as that. And then we'd go right up under, right through this dressing room right back, see, and then go up on the stage and do stage presentation. And so we usually reported around one o'clock, we'd go up around ten minutes to eleven, something like that. We usually did three shows sometime, four, according to how the business was, you know. So I guess Louis was hearing about me all the time because when he hit Chicago, he chews me, which would cause a lot of jealousy, you know. Well, that's when he's homeboy, you see. That's homeboy, see. They look out for one another. They always did look out for one another.
